question: Why are columnar storage engines 10x-100x faster for analytical aggregations than row stores? Why are columnar storage engines 10x-100x faster for analytical aggregations than row stores?

options.text: Columnar stores read only the specific columns referenced in queries and use CPU SIMD vectorization to process thousands of values per instruction.

Columnar stores compress every column with the same universal algorithm regardless of data type, and it is this uniform compression alone that produces the speedup, independent of which columns are read.
Columnar stores keep a full row-oriented copy in memory at all times as a cache, and only fall back to the column-oriented disk layout when memory pressure is high.
Columnar stores achieve their speed by pre-computing every possible aggregation (SUM, AVG, COUNT) at write time, so a query only ever looks up a cached result.

explanation: Specification answer: Columnar stores read only the specific columns referenced in queries and use CPU SIMD vectorization to process thousands of values per instruction.

question: What is Vectorized Execution in DuckDB? What is Vectorized Execution in DuckDB?

options.text: Processing data in batches of columnar vectors (e.g. 2,048 values in CPU L1/L2 cache) rather than executing an iterator loop one tuple at a time.
It compiles each SQL query into native machine code ahead of time, avoiding an interpreter loop entirely, regardless of how many rows are processed at once.
It processes one entire column's full set of values as a single batch across the whole table, no matter how large the table is, rather than a small fixed-size chunk.
It runs each query stage on a separate CPU core in parallel, and 'vectorized' refers to distributing rows across cores rather than to batching within a single core.

explanation: Specification answer: Processing data in batches of columnar vectors (e.g. 2,048 values in CPU L1/L2 cache) rather than executing an iterator loop one tuple at a time.

question: How does the ClickHouse MergeTree storage engine organize data on disk? How does the ClickHouse MergeTree storage engine organize data on disk?

options.text: It sorts data by primary key, writes immutable sorted column parts, and merges them asynchronously in the background.
It stores each inserted row immediately in its final sorted position within one single ever-growing file, updating that file in place on every insert.
It partitions data only by primary key range and never merges parts in the background; compaction is triggered exclusively by a manual OPTIMIZE TABLE command.
It keeps all data unsorted in insertion order and instead relies entirely on a secondary B-Tree index over the primary key for fast lookups.

explanation: Specification answer: It sorts data by primary key, writes immutable sorted column parts, and merges them asynchronously in the background.

question: What is Parquet predicate pushdown and projection pushdown? What is Parquet predicate pushdown and projection pushdown?

options.text: Projection pushdown reads only requested columns; predicate pushdown uses row-group min/max statistics to skip entire chunks of data without decompression.
Predicate pushdown reads only requested columns; projection pushdown uses row-group statistics to skip chunks without decompression, which is the reverse pairing of terms and functions.
Both pushdown types only apply after the entire file has already been fully decompressed into memory, so they save CPU time but never save I/O.
Projection pushdown filters rows using min/max statistics per row group, while predicate pushdown determines which columns to decompress from disk.

explanation: Specification answer: Projection pushdown reads only requested columns; predicate pushdown uses row-group min/max statistics to skip entire chunks of data without decompression.

question:
During triage in Columnar OLAP DuckDB ClickHouse, an engineer observes:
"System fault during operation: DB::Exception: Too Many Parts in Table in ClickHouse".
What is the verified root cause?

options.text: Microservice sends 5,000 single-row HTTP INSERT requests per second to ClickHouse MergeTree, exhausting background merge worker capacity.
The table's ORDER BY key is set to a column with extremely high cardinality, and 'Too Many Parts' is actually a symptom of too many distinct sort-key values, not of insert frequency.
A single INSERT statement with 5,000,000 rows was issued, and ClickHouse splits any INSERT above 1,000,000 rows into one part per row before merging, regardless of how the insert was batched.
Background merges are disabled because the table was created with the Log engine instead of MergeTree, so parts accumulate because no merge process exists at all for this engine.

explanation:
Root Cause: Microservice sends 5,000 single-row HTTP INSERT requests per second to ClickHouse MergeTree, exhausting background merge worker capacity.

Fix Resolution:
Batch inserts into chunks of at least 10,000 rows before sending to ClickHouse, or insert into a Buffer engine table.
